# Load the UN General Debate Corpus
```{r}
library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.corpora)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

data("data_corpus_ungd2017",
     package = "quanteda.corpora")

un <- data_corpus_ungd2017
rm(data_corpus_ungd2017)

# Remove missing observations
un <- un |>
  convert(to = "data.frame") |>
  drop_na(continent, gdp_per_capita)

# Check the number of statements
dim(un)
```

# Text preprocessing
```{r}
library(stringi)
library(textclean)
library(dplyr)

un <- un |>
  mutate(
    text.clean = stri_trans_general(
      text,
      id = "Any-Latin;Latin-ASCII"
    ),
    text.clean = tolower(text.clean),
    text.clean = replace_curly_quote(text.clean),
    text.clean = replace_contraction(text.clean),
    text.clean = gsub("[[:digit:]]+", " ", text.clean),
    text.clean = gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", text.clean),
    text.clean = trimws(text.clean)
  )

# Check the results
dim(un)
substr(un$text.clean[1], 1, 200)

```

#Lemmatisation
```{r}

library(udpipe)
library(tidytext)
library(dplyr)

# Find an existing English model
model_files <- list.files(
  pattern = "^english-gum.*\\.udpipe$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

# Download the model only if necessary
if (length(model_files) == 0) {
  eng <- udpipe_download_model(language = "english-gum")
  model_file <- eng$file_model
} else {
  model_file <- model_files[1]
}

# Load the model
ud_eng <- udpipe_load_model(model_file)


# Lemmatization
un.df.trip <- udpipe_annotate(
  x = un$text.clean,
  object = ud_eng
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = c("lemma" = "word")) |>
  select(doc_id, lemma) |>
  filter(!grepl("[[:punct:]]+", lemma)) |>
  count(doc_id, lemma)
  
  
dim(un.df.trip)
head(un.df.trip, 10)
```

# Document-term matrix
```{r}
un.dtm <- un.df.trip |>
  cast_dfm(
    document = doc_id,
    term = lemma,
    value = n
  ) |>
  dfm_trim(
    min_docfreq = 0.1,
    max_docfreq = 0.9,
    docfreq_type = "prop"
  )

# Check dimensions
dim(un.dtm)
```
```{r}
# Align metadata with the document-term matrix
rownames(un) <- paste0("doc", 1:nrow(un))

un <- un[rownames(un.dtm), ]

# Verify alignment
identical(rownames(un), rownames(un.dtm))
```
```{r}
# Check document identifiers
head(un$doc_id)

# Check dimensions
dim(un)
dim(un.dtm)
```

#Embeddings fast text
```{r}

library(text2map.pretrained)


# Load pretrained fastText embeddings
wv <- text2map.pretrained::load_pretrained(
  "vecs_fasttext300_commoncrawl"
)

# Keep only vectors corresponding to DTM lemmas
un.vectors <- wv[
  rownames(wv) %in% colnames(un.dtm),
]


dim(un.vectors)

```

#Part I: Semantic Directions
##Question 1
```{r}
# Load required package
library(text2map)
library(dplyr)

# Retrieve policy anchor words
anchors <- text2map::get_anchors("policy")

# Display the first anchor pairs
head(anchors)

```

```{r}
# Keep only anchor pairs available in the embeddings
anchors <- anchors[
  anchors$pole1 %in% rownames(un.vectors),
]

anchors <- anchors[
  anchors$pole2 %in% rownames(un.vectors),
]

# Check remaining anchor pairs
anchors
```

```{r}
# Construct the policy semantic direction
policy.direction <- text2map::get_direction(
  anchors = anchors,
  wv = un.vectors
)

# Check the dimensions
dim(policy.direction)
```
##Question 2
```{r}
# Calculate cosine similarity with the semantic direction

direction <- as.numeric(policy.direction[1, ])

cosine_scores <- as.numeric(
  un.vectors %*% direction
) / (
  sqrt(rowSums(un.vectors^2)) *
  sqrt(sum(direction^2))
)

# Create a data frame with lemmas and cosine scores

cosine_results <- data.frame(
  lemma = rownames(un.vectors),
  cosine = cosine_scores
)
```

```{r}
# Top 10 words closest to the domestic pole
top_domestic <- cosine_results |>
  arrange(desc(cosine)) |>
  head(10)

print(top_domestic)

# Top 10 words closest to the foreign pole
top_foreign <- cosine_results |>
  arrange(cosine) |>
  head(10)

print(top_foreign)
```

##Question 3
The semantic direction reveals an asymmetry between the two poles. Words associated with the foreign pole, such as diplomatic, delegation, envoy, and ambassador, form a relatively coherent vocabulary related to international relations and diplomacy.

In contrast, the domestic pole is more heterogeneous. Although terms such as violence, abuse, and tragedy may refer to domestic challenges, other words, including ongoing, range, and capacity, are less clearly associated with domestic policy.

These results suggest that the semantic direction captures the foreign policy dimension more clearly than the domestic one. However, the interpretation should remain cautious because only one pair of anchor words (domestic/foreign) was available after filtering.

#Part 2: Word Mover’s Distance
##Question 1

```{r}
# Load required package
library(text2vec)

# Identify vocabulary covered by the embeddings
vocab <- rownames(un.vectors)

# Restrict the DTM to the available vocabulary
un.dtm.wmd <- un.dtm[, vocab]

# Assign country names to the rows
rownames(un.dtm.wmd) <- un$doc_id

# Check dimensions
dim(un.dtm.wmd)
```
```{r}
# Create the RWMD model
wmd_mod <- RWMD$new(
  x = un.dtm.wmd,
  embeddings = un.vectors
)

# Compute document similarities
wmd_dis <- wmd_mod$sim2(x = un.dtm.wmd)

# Check dimensions
dim(wmd_dis)

# Display a subset of the similarity matrix
wmd_dis[1:5, 1:5]

```
##Question 2
```{r}
# Load required packages
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(reshape2)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

# Visualize similarities to the United States and China
wmd_dis[c("United States", "China"), ] |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "country") |>
  reshape2::melt() |>
  filter(
    !(country == "United States" & variable == "United States") &
    !(country == "China" & variable == "China")
  ) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  mutate(
    label = ifelse(
      value >= quantile(value, .9) |
      value <= quantile(value, .1),
      country,
      NA
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = .3) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = label),
    alpha = .5,
    max.overlaps = Inf
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "Word Mover's Distance",
    x = ""
  )
```
###Additional visualization

To improve the readability of the figure, I produced an additional visualization highlighting only the five countries with the highest and lowest similarity scores for each reference country (United States and China). This adjustment reduces label overlap while preserving the original similarity scores and distributions.
```{r}

# Prepare data for visualization
wmd_plot <- wmd_dis[c("United States", "China"), ] |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "country") |>
  reshape2::melt(
    id.vars = "country",
    variable.name = "reference_country"
  ) |>
  filter(
    !(country == "United States" &
        reference_country == "United States"),
    !(country == "China" &
        reference_country == "China")
  ) |>
  group_by(reference_country) |>
  mutate(
    rank_high = min_rank(desc(value)),
    rank_low = min_rank(value),
    label = ifelse(
      rank_high <= 5 | rank_low <= 5,
      country,
      NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Plot

#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(wmd_plot,
       aes(x = reference_country, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "mediumpurple3",
    alpha = 0.3,
    width = 0.45,
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = label),
    na.rm = TRUE,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    size = 3,
    box.padding = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Semantic Similarity to US and Chinese UN Speeches",
    subtitle = "UN General Debate Corpus, 2017",
    x = "",
    y = "RWMD Similarity Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```
The figure shows that the United States generally has higher semantic similarity scores with other countries' UN General Debate statements than China. The median similarity is approximately 0.79 for the United States, compared with 0.75 for China.

The countries displaying the highest similarities also differ between the two reference countries. For instance, Czechia and Israel appear among the most similar to the United States, whereas South Korea, Japan, and Vietnam show high similarity scores with China.

These findings suggest that the two speeches share vocabulary and semantic content with different sets of countries. However, semantic similarity does not necessarily imply political or diplomatic agreement. Countries may discuss similar international issues while adopting different positions.

#On Your Own
##Question 1
Selected dimension: Economy vs. Environment

##Question 2
```{r}
# Create anchor words for Economy vs. Environment

anchors_econ_env <- data.frame(
  pole1 = c(
    "economy",
    "growth",
    "investment",
    "trade",
    "industry"
  ),
  pole2 = c(
    "climate",
    "environment",
    "biodiversity",
    "pollution",
    "sustainability"
  )
)

# Display the anchor pairs
anchors_econ_env
```

```{r}
# Check availability of anchor words

anchors_econ_env |>
  mutate(
    pole1_available = pole1 %in% rownames(un.vectors),
    pole2_available = pole2 %in% rownames(un.vectors)
  )
```
```{r}
# Check alternative environmental anchor words

alternatives <- c(
  "conservation",
  "emission",
  "ecosystem"
)

data.frame(
  word = alternatives,
  available = alternatives %in% rownames(un.vectors)
)
```

```{r}
# Replace pollution with conservation
anchors_econ_env$pole2[
  anchors_econ_env$pole2 == "pollution"
] <- "conservation"

# Keep only anchor pairs available in the embeddings
anchors_econ_env <- anchors_econ_env[
  anchors_econ_env$pole1 %in% rownames(un.vectors) &
  anchors_econ_env$pole2 %in% rownames(un.vectors),
]

# Check the final anchor list
anchors_econ_env

# Construct the Economy vs. Environment semantic direction
econ_env.direction <- text2map::get_direction(
  anchors = anchors_econ_env,
  wv = un.vectors
)

# Check dimensions
dim(econ_env.direction)
```

##Question 3
```{r}
# Extract the semantic direction
direction_econ_env <- as.numeric(econ_env.direction[1, ])

# Calculate cosine similarities
cosine_scores_econ_env <- as.numeric(
  un.vectors %*% direction_econ_env
) / (
  sqrt(rowSums(un.vectors^2)) *
  sqrt(sum(direction_econ_env^2))
)

# Create a data frame with lemmas and cosine scores
cosine_results_econ_env <- data.frame(
  lemma = rownames(un.vectors),
  cosine = cosine_scores_econ_env
)
```

```{r}
# Top 10 lemmas closest to the Economy pole
top_economy <- cosine_results_econ_env |>
  arrange(desc(cosine)) |>
  head(10)

print(top_economy)

# Top 10 lemmas closest to the Environment pole
top_environment <- cosine_results_econ_env |>
  arrange(cosine) |>
  head(10)

print(top_environment)
```
##Question 4
I chose to construct a semantic direction contrasting economy and environment, as both dimensions are central to international discussions on development and sustainability. For the economic pole, I selected economy, growth, investment, trade, and industry. For the environmental pole, I selected climate, environment, biodiversity, conservation, and sustainability.

The results reveal two relatively coherent semantic fields. The economic pole is associated with terms such as market, sector, employment, and business, suggesting a focus on economic activity, production, and employment. In contrast, the environmental pole includes words such as environmental, warming, earth, and science, reflecting concerns related to climate change and environmental protection.

However, the economic pole shows stronger cosine scores than the environmental pole. This difference should be interpreted cautiously, as the scores measure semantic associations rather than the frequency or importance of these issues in UN speeches. Furthermore, economy and environment are not necessarily opposing policy objectives, particularly in discussions of sustainable development.
